Q.c: The CPU runs programs using the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Q.q: Describe the fetch stage of the cycle. You may use register transfer notation in your answer.

pts: MAR ← [PC]: the address in the PC is copied to the MAR
The address is placed on the address bus and a memory read signal is sent on the control bus
MBR ← [Memory] addressed by the MAR: the instruction travels on the data bus into the MBR
PC ← [PC] + 1: the PC is incremented to point to the next instruction
CIR ← [MBR]: the instruction is copied into the CIR
g: Steps must be in a sensible order for full marks.

Q.c: The console uses the von Neumann architecture.
Q.q: Explain one drawback of the von Neumann architecture.

ms.h: One mark for the drawback, one for the linked explanation:
pts: Instructions and data share the same memory and the same buses …
… so an instruction and data cannot be fetched at the same time, which limits the speed of the CPU (the von Neumann bottleneck)
g: Also accept: data can overwrite instructions because they are stored in the same memory (1) … so a bug or attack can change the program (1).

Q.c: The console's CPU has level 1, level 2 and level 3 cache as well as 16 GiB of RAM.
Q.q: Explain why the CPU has several levels of cache rather than relying on RAM alone.

pts: RAM is much slower than the CPU, so the CPU would often wait for data
Cache is faster than RAM / closer to the CPU
Cache holds copies of frequently used / recently used instructions and data
Most requests are found in cache (hits) so the CPU waits less
Fast memory is expensive, so small fast levels (L1) are combined with larger, slower, cheaper levels (L2, L3)

Q.c: While a video is being exported, the user presses a key on the keyboard.

pts: The keyboard controller sets a bit in the interrupt register
The CPU checks for interrupts at the end of each fetch-decode-execute cycle
The priority of the interrupt is compared with the current task
The contents of the registers (including the PC) are saved on the stack
The PC is loaded with the address of the interrupt service routine (ISR) for the keyboard
The ISR runs (e.g. reads the key code into a buffer)
The saved register values are restored from the stack and the original task continues

Pages not currently in use are swapped out to secondary storage and swapped back when needed
Secondary storage is much slower than RAM
If pages are swapped in and out constantly, the computer spends more time swapping than processing (disk thrashing)

Parallel wires suffer crosstalk / interference between them
Serial can be clocked much faster, so it can still achieve a high transfer rate
Serial needs fewer wires, so the cable is cheaper / thinner

Pages can be placed in any free frames; a page table maps pages to frames
A page may split a routine in two; a segment keeps a logical unit together
Segmentation can leave gaps between segments in memory

Q.c: The café's card machine uses symmetric encryption to send payments to the bank.

pts: The same key is used to encrypt and to decrypt
Plaintext is encrypted with the key to give ciphertext, and the bank decrypts it with the same key
Both sides must have the key before communicating
The problem is key exchange: the key must be shared securely, as anyone who intercepts it can decrypt the data
